title: 6174, Kaprekar's constant
hook: Shuffle almost any four-digit number this way and you always land on 6174.
peek: Arrange a four-digit number's digits from largest to smallest, subtract the reverse, and repeat. Whatever you start with, as long as the digits are not all the same, you reach 6174 within seven steps, and then you are stuck there.
lede: Pick a four-digit number whose digits are not all the same, such as 3524. Arrange its digits from largest to smallest, 5432, and from smallest to largest, 2345, then subtract: 3087. Do it again with the answer, and again. Within at most seven rounds you reach 6174, and from there the process only ever gives 6174 back.

bullets.text: From 3524 the steps run 3087, then 8730 minus 0378 gives 8352, then 8532 minus 2358 gives 6174. Three rounds, and you are home. Keeping leading zeros, so 378 counts as 0378, matters for the rule to work.
The number fixes itself: its digits sorted high to low make 7641 and low to high make 1467, and 7641 minus 1467 is 6174 again. No other four-digit result does that.
Dattatreya Ramchandra Kaprekar was a schoolteacher in Devlali, India, who explored number patterns in his spare time. He described the routine in 1949, and the constant now carries his name.
With three-digit numbers the same routine always ends at 495. For five or more digits there is no single landing point, and numbers fall into loops or one of several end points instead.
Numbers like 1111 or 7777 are the only exceptions. Sorting gives the same number both ways, so the first subtraction lands on 0 and stays there.
